meta.home: I'm Lorenzo. I build software for the parts of a business that are still being done by hand. You don't need to know what should be built. Tell me what isn't working and I'll help work out the rest.
meta.work: Four things I've been trusted to build: a travel eSIM used all over the world, software that watches camera feeds for a living, my own product, and a course I wrote. For each one: the situation, what I did, and the part that was genuinely hard.
meta.about: What it's like to work with me, how I think about a problem before I build anything, and a bit about who I am.

hero.status: Open to a couple of projects
hero.lede: I'm Lorenzo. People come to me when something in their business is slow, repetitive, or stuck in a spreadsheet only one person really understands. You don't need to know what should be built. Working that out is the job.

facts.latestValue: AInterest, live and open to anyone

capabilities.title: You don't need to know what to build.
capabilities.lede: Most people get in touch with a description of something that isn't working. A process that takes too long. Information one person retypes into a second system every morning. An idea that so far only exists in someone's head. That's enough to start from. Sometimes the answer turns out not to be software at all, and I'll say so.

manualWork.title: Work your team still does by hand
manualWork.body: The report someone rebuilds every Monday morning. Numbers retyped from one system into another. Work that repeats so often nobody really reads it any more. Software can take that part, and your people get the time back.

customTool.title: The tool you wish existed
customTool.body: Most businesses do something in a way no ready-made product handles properly, so it ends up split between a few spreadsheets, a shared inbox and whatever one person keeps in their head. This is the thing built around the way you already work.

ideaToProduct.title: An idea that needs to become a product
ideaToProduct.body: You have something in your head and no clear picture yet of what it looks like. I've done this with my own product, from the first idea to something anyone can sign up for today, so you can go and see how it turned out.

systemsTalking.title: Tools that don't talk to each other
systemsTalking.body: Your accounting software, the system the sales team lives in, a supplier's website, something old that nobody wants to touch. Getting information to move between them on its own, and getting it right often enough that people stop checking it by hand.

aiWhereItPays.title: AI where it genuinely saves time
aiWhereItPays.body: I've built AI into a product people use, and I teach a course on working with these tools. That's also why I'll tell you when it's an expensive way to solve something that doesn't need it.

outgrown.title: Something you've outgrown
outgrown.body: It still works, but every small change takes weeks, everyone has their own workaround, and nobody wants to be the person who breaks it. Sometimes that's worth fixing and sometimes it's worth starting again. I'll tell you honestly which one I think it is.

work.title: Four things I've been trusted to build.
work.lede: A travel eSIM sold under the FC Barcelona name, software that watches camera feeds for a living, a product of my own, and a course I wrote. Different problems, same job underneath.
work.pageTitle: Four things I've been trusted to build.
work.pageLede: Not a list of everything I've ever made. These four, because between them they answer the question people actually have: what was the situation, what did I do about it, what was hard, and what does that say about handing me a problem of your own.

course.formatValue: Online, recorded, at your own pace
course.lengthValue: Two modules, eleven lessons, about four weeks
course.note: It's the only thing here that isn't software. It's on the list because being able to explain something clearly, to people who will go and test it that evening, is a different skill from being able to build it — and it's the reason I'll tell you when AI isn't the answer to your problem.

barcaMobile.summary: A travel eSIM sold under the FC Barcelona name. The product I work on day to day.
barcaMobile.situation: Getting online in another country is still a small ordeal: a bill you find out about afterwards, or a queue at an airport shop. Barça Mobile sells mobile data in over 170 countries, and it does it under a name people already recognise, which sets the bar for how it has to feel. The person using it is usually standing in a terminal with no signal yet and no patience for a screen that needs working out.
barcaMobile.contribution: I'm a senior engineer on the team that builds it, and I work across the product rather than one corner of it: the app people manage their plan in, the site where they choose one, and the parts behind both. In practice that's picking a destination, buying a plan, getting the eSIM onto the phone and seeing how much data is left — the moments where somebody either gets connected or gives up and walks to a shop.
barcaMobile.challenge: Nothing ships because it worked on my machine. Installing an eSIM is the unforgiving step: it happens once, on a phone the person has never set up this way, usually on borrowed airport wifi, and if it goes wrong they don't try again. So most of the care goes into a small number of screens where things can quietly go wrong, and into being sure a change hasn't broken something for the people already using it.
barcaMobile.proof: I spend my working week inside a real product with paying customers and a brand attached. That's a different discipline from building something and moving on — release after release, other people's code, decisions you have to defend, and problems that surface long after you thought you were finished. It's also where I learned that the last ten per cent is the part everyone underestimates.
barcaMobile.role: Senior software engineer on the product team, across the app, the site and what sits behind them.

examin.summary: Software that watches camera feeds and tells people what just happened.
examin.situation: Plenty of businesses already have cameras everywhere and nobody with the time to watch them. A cracked solar panel, a pallet in the wrong place, someone in an area they shouldn't be in — all of it is on camera, and all of it gets noticed hours later, if at all. Examin turns cameras a company already owns into something that says what happened while it's still happening, across jobs as different as checking solar farms and reading number plates.
examin.contribution: I was brought in to build the product, not to decorate it. That means everything the person on shift touches — the live views, the alerts, the evidence attached to each one, the settings that decide what is worth interrupting someone for — along with the work underneath that keeps it all connected to the cameras and the detections coming out of them. I was also part of deciding what the product should be, rather than being handed a finished specification.
examin.challenge: Restraint. Software like this can flag almost anything, and an alert nobody trusts is worse than no alert at all — people mute it inside a week. So a lot of the work was about what not to show, and about what somebody needs in the one second they spend deciding whether to believe it: the actual frame, the time, how certain the system is. Then making one product cover very different industries without turning into a settings screen nobody can face.
examin.proof: Someone handed me a genuinely complicated product and let me help decide what it should be. If what you have is a vague sense that something in your process is being missed, and no clear idea what the answer looks like, this is exactly the shape of problem I'm comfortable being given.
examin.role: Brought in as the developer: the product people use, the parts behind it, and a say in what got built.

ainterest.summary: My own product. Make images with AI, then put them somewhere other people can see them.
ainterest.situation: Nobody asked for this one. Every tool for making images with AI buries the results in a chat window — whatever you made last week is gone unless you thought to save it yourself, and you never get to see what anyone else is doing. That seemed like the wrong shape for something people mostly do for the pleasure of it.
ainterest.contribution: I built the whole thing and it's live. You describe what you want and you get an image; everything you make stays in your account; you can publish any of it to a feed other people browse and search. Accounts, generation, the feed, what it costs to keep running — all of it mine. There was no specification, because there was nobody to write one.
ainterest.challenge: Almost none of the difficulty was the AI. Making one image is slow, costs real money every single time, and sometimes simply fails. The app has to be honest about that while you wait without looking broken, and stay quick as the feed fills up. Every wrong decision was one I paid for myself that month, which is a fast way to learn which decisions matter.
ainterest.proof: This is the one that answers whether I can do more than build what I'm told. Somebody had to decide what it was, what to leave out, what happens when things fail, and when it was good enough to put a stranger in front of. Your project needs that same set of decisions made, and here they were all mine.
ainterest.role: Mine, start to finish: the idea, every product decision, the build, and the bills.

aiForFrontend.summary: An online course teaching developers to work with AI properly. I wrote it and I teach it.
aiForFrontend.situation: Developers picked up AI tools in a hurry and started using them by feel. Some of it saves an absurd amount of time. Some of it quietly eats an afternoon and hands you something that looks right and isn't. What was missing was anybody willing to say plainly where that line falls.
aiForFrontend.contribution: I decided what the course covers, wrote every example and recorded all of it. Two modules and eleven lessons: how these tools actually work and where they mislead you, how to ask for something and get back something usable, how to use them on real work — someone else's code, finding bugs, tests, documentation — and how to do all that without giving up the judgement that made you worth hiring in the first place. It's published by Itlogia, a licensed online school, and it's available now.
aiForFrontend.challenge: These tools change every few months. Teach the tools and the course is out of date before anyone finishes it, so I taught the habits instead: what to check, what never to trust, where a person still has to think. Getting that across meant working out what I actually believed, which is harder than it sounds when you've been doing it on instinct.
aiForFrontend.proof: Teaching is a stricter test than being good at something. You can't hide a vague explanation from people who will go and try it themselves that evening. It's also why I'll tell you when AI isn't the answer to your problem: I had to write down exactly where these tools stop being useful.
aiForFrontend.role: Author and instructor. I chose what it covers, wrote the material and recorded every lesson.

process.title: You talk to the person building it.
process.lede: No account manager, and nobody you've never met doing the actual work.

understand.title: Work out the real problem
understand.body: A conversation and a lot of questions about how the work happens now. Quite often what's worth building isn't what was asked for, and that's a much cheaper thing to find out at the start.

scope.title: Agree the smallest useful version
scope.body: What gets built first, what it costs, and what we're leaving out on purpose. You get all of that in writing before any work starts.

build.title: Build it where you can see it
build.body: You get something you can click through long before it's finished. Changing your mind is cheap at the start and expensive at the end, so tell me early.

handOver.title: Hand it over properly
handOver.body: It goes live, it's written down, and it belongs to you. You shouldn't have to pay me every month for it to keep working. I'm around if you want me, not because you're stuck with me.

aboutTeaser.title: One person, start to finish.
aboutTeaser.body1: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I work as a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I take on a small number of client projects alongside it. I'm also finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
aboutTeaser.body2: I've been building software for years and I've done every part of it, from the screens people click on to everything running quietly behind them. Which tools that takes is my problem to work out, not something you need an opinion about.
aboutTeaser.body3: So one person holds the whole thing, from the first conversation about what's going wrong to the version your team opens on a Monday morning.

contact.title: Tell me what isn't working.
contact.lede: You don't need a document, a budget, or a clear idea of what to build. A couple of sentences about what's going wrong is plenty. If I think it isn't worth building, or that someone else would do it better, I'll tell you that too.

about.title: The longer version.
about.lede: How I work, how I decide what's worth building, and what I'm like to deal with.
about.intro: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I'm a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I'm finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
about.freelance: Alongside that I take on a few client projects and keep my own products running. That's where I try things out before they go anywhere near someone else's business.
about.career: Most of what I've built ended up in front of real people, which teaches you quickly. You find out within a day if something is confusing. I've also looked after the parts nobody ever sees, the ones that decide whether the thing still works at four on a Friday afternoon.
about.interests: The part I enjoy most happens before any of that, sitting with a problem until it's clear what should exist. Plenty of people can build what you describe. Fewer will tell you that what you described isn't quite what you need.

principles.title: A few things I believe about building software.

problem.title: The brief is a guess
problem.body: People ask for solutions, because that's easier than describing a problem. So the first thing I do is work backwards to what's actually wrong, then check that the thing you asked for would fix it.

smallest.title: Start with the smallest useful thing
smallest.body: A small version people are already using tells you more than a big version described in a document. It's also how you avoid paying twice for the wrong thing.

maintainable.title: Someone has to live with this
maintainable.body: Whatever I build has to make sense to whoever looks at it next, and that might well be you. Clever solutions are usually just harder to fix later.

ai.title: AI is a tool, not a plan
ai.body: I use these tools every day and recorded a course on them. That's exactly why I'll say so when the answer to your problem isn't AI at all.

working.title: What working with me usually looks like.
working.intro: The things people tend to want to know before they get in touch.

noSpec.label: You don't have a plan
noSpec.body: That's the normal case. Almost nobody arrives with one. Telling me what's slow, or what keeps going wrong, is a better start than a document guessing at the answer.

notSure.label: Not sure it's software
notSure.body: Sometimes it isn't, and I'll tell you. Changing how something is done, or turning on a setting in software you already pay for, is often the better answer.

tooSmall.label: It feels too small
tooSmall.body: A week of work that takes away something your team does every single day is a good project. I'd take that over a six-month plan that never gets finished.

existing.label: Something already exists
existing.body: I can pick up what's there, finish something that stalled, or work alongside whoever built it. I'd rather not throw away something you've already paid for.

managing.label: You don't want to manage a developer
managing.body: You shouldn't have to. I'll ask when I genuinely need an answer and get on with it the rest of the time, and you'll see where things are without having to chase me.

money.label: Cost and timing
money.body: You get a price and a date before any work starts. If either one is going to move, you hear it from me while there's still time to do something about it.

outro.title: Away from the screen.
outro.body: I read more newsletters than is reasonable, and I spend a lot of my own time making things with no purpose at all. No client, no deadline, nobody asking for it. That's mostly the appeal.
